After a couple of runs, I lost interest. The game is cute yet mediocre. They tried to go the Brotato way, alas, Brotato could get away with monotone arenas by having a flexible progression system coupled with drastically different playstyles provided by its distinct gimmicky characters. And the shooting was fun. This mimic doesn't come close in complexity or gratification, despite having a ton of stats. As a substitute for interesting mechanics, here you buy some bloody seeds, you plant them, water them, get the coin, weapons, or exp. Repeat. Depending on a character, you may also be mining or fishing, and you're always fighting. All of the activities involve mostly shuffling in place while listening to understated rustling, whooshing, and feeble jingles. As for character abilities, those normally range from +2% X per occupied farming plot to "can't mine well", that kind of inanity. Even when it's not so boring, it's all the same so it gets old fast. Although, the power creep exists and it's mildly pleasant. I can't say this game lacks everything that makes a good VS clone. There's some strategy involved, it can kill you some time. I believe it to be a well-intended project. However, it matters not, for none of the activities pop audiovisually. The sprites are fine, but the enemies all blend into an insipid clump of nothingness, having no discernible abilities that matter. They're bugs, but they don't even crunch properly! Most of the weapon effects and projectiles are barely noticeable, so are the damage numbers. Mowing the hordes doesn't feel satisfying, it just mellowly happens in the background while you go around your stupid farming business, a dubious gimmick that adds an unnecessary extra step between killing and level rewards. It also lacks the oomph. I know it ain't easy to make planting seeds or fishing feel impactful, but it seems like the challenge wasn't attempted at all. No effort was put into making the menial tasks that constitute the whole game adhere to the bullet heaven standards. I don't see how these vital aspects could get better later on. But it's good achievement hunting fodder, I guess? Oh, those you'll find here in droves! If nothing else. Its a very charming, very cute survivors game. Its even got some interesting things going for it in terms of different characters having different objectives. I like a lot about this game, but sadly it just misses the plot on a few key components of the genre that make it more frustrating than fun after a few runs. -The hit boxes are a little wonky, meaning its its *very* difficult to juke through mobs without taking damage. -This is extra noticeable because most of the weapons are *terrible*, and unless you are taking the few good weapons and prioritizing exclusively damage upgrades, you *will* get completely overwhelmed on difficulty 3 & 4. -There just isn't a lot of variety? The weapons don't combine/transform, there are only a few pet types, very limited strategy when it comes to farming, and the upgrades are all just number go up bundles, meaning no given upgrade is all that exciting. -One map, never changes, one track, never changes. If it was $4 or less, I'd say sure. But unless you are just here for the cute frogs (who are very cute), I'd say pass.

Only few weapons. Even music is just boring and makes you want to fall asleep. If you are looking for a slow game with almost no progression and content then grab it. Otherwise avoid this title.

因为开发路径基本透明，市场上充斥着各种类吸血鬼游戏，也延伸出多款变种，但无论如何，都脱离不开体验——而最直观的体验就是：这款游戏是否玩不腻。青蛙农场给的答案无疑是很肯定的——无论是从局内种田养成的玩法、风格主题还是角色设计，这款游戏都能在保有基本游戏体验的同时做出些许创新。 和类吸血鬼模式一样，青蛙农场也保留着局内rouge割草，局外升级解锁的基本玩法，战斗系统偏向纯粹的短刃战（敌人的攻击方式非弹幕类）。不过，游戏最大的特色莫过于局内种田养成。在指定的交互物附近待上一段时间，角色便能够与之交互——矿石、钓鱼点能够获得相应的奖励，而农田则可以播种、间歇浇水维持作物成长，收获作物获得经验值与武器。正因为交互行为较多，角色的行动模式不再是普通的“走位、杀怪、升级”，同时还要规划路线，兼顾任何能让角色成长的因素。另外，大多数武器都是围绕角色360°的大风车式进攻，当游戏进行到中后期时，数值成长的快感直接反映在了视觉的夸张攻击效果上，非常魔性，补足了不少简略图形和进攻判定上的缺陷。 总体非常推荐，也是半年来玩得较上头的一款类吸血鬼肉鸽。值得入手。 [h1] [quote] [table] [tr] [th] 🐱😸[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45217105][b] 不羁猫探索队 [/b][/url] | [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44339075][b] 不羁猫外文站 [/b][/url]😸🐱 [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 🧶🧶致力小型独游双语推广，主评叙事/策略类游戏🧶🧶 [/th] [/tr] [tr] [tr] [th] 欢迎开发者和小伙伴们一起交流 无限进步ฅ●ω●ฅ [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/untamecat][b] 联系我们[/b][/url] |[url=https://indienova.com/author/mGvZ4JrvB86518/][b] 相关文章[/b][/url] [/th] [/tr]

[h1]蛙天帝之农场保卫战[/h1] 众生有所不知，各类害虫尽是农场之敌，今日我蛙天地立下宏远，蛙在田在，田毁蛙亡，呱～就仿佛那愚公移山，自己没了还有后代，今日吾呱亦是如此，终有一日，还农田朗朗乾坤！ 《青蛙农场：幸存者》顾名思义是以青蛙为主体的幸存者肉鸽游戏。与以往的幸存者游戏比较，本作杀敌不再会掉落经验，取而代之的是种田钓鱼可以获得经验，又因为敌人是源源不断，而种田和钓鱼有成型时间，这就造成了，升级有危险，吃东西需谨慎 这种特别的运行模式，让我对这款幸存者很感兴趣。游戏中除了宠物，所有东西需要种植才可以获得，无论是武器还是经验。除了武器会自然生长，所有的植物都能有多流程，种植，浇水，收割然后获得经验。武器最多五级，然后游戏有融合手册，两个五级武器可以融合新的武器，我个人最喜欢舌鞭加长剑合成次元斩，虽然攻击cd长但是基本全屏秒杀。 游戏目前现在有四个主题（春夏秋冬），每个主题有四个难度，然后怪物的种类也多种多样，以各种常见虫子为主（天牛，蝗虫）还有各种我不认识的，现实中虫子危害越大，游戏里虫子越强。 目前游戏可玩角色有几十个，都是通过成就解锁的，开局的初始蛙以平衡为主，后面各种族人出现，能力各不相同，都是为了守护农田出一份力。我爱幸存者，我爱青蛙~ [quote] 亲亲亲！亲亲亲！噗铃噗铃！爱你爱你！姆尼姆尼！叻咯叻咯！姆拉姆拉！[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44515001]不动不动不动卿[/url]亲亲亲！亲亲亲！爱你爱你！姆尼姆尼！噗铃噗铃！波隆奴璐璐！叻咯叻咯！ [/quote]
这是一款打着割草爽游旗号然后把割草玩家骗进来杀的游戏，几乎绝大部分的升级选项都有着负面词缀，同时他的词条又非常的多，显得很杂乱，很多时候你只能随便瞎选，因为你很难去记得他们都有什么功能。同时很多人物弱的跟得了脑血栓一样，点名医生蛙（说实话我很怀疑制作组内是不是有人被医生绿了）。 总之这是一款我很不推荐的游戏，它存在的意义就是肆无忌惮的向玩家展示制作组的恶意。

Mixed feelings. Great concept spoiled by balancing. + plenty stuff to collect: characters that all play different, achivements that encourage different playstyles, meta upgrades expensive and niche enough to not make you op + farming didn't sound like a great addition, but it actually narrows the map down to your farm, encourages movement between the crops and the well, always forces descisions like "do I want to fish or water stuff or mine stuff now?" + enemies are visible in front of the background, there's no red aoe clutter that ruins many other bullethells I've played, your weapon effects are (mostly) subtle enough to not make me want to ask for opacity settings - it's just the bucket soemtimes blocking my view + upgrades all come with a trade off: that's important because it makes you think about your priorities, sort of like risk and reward & and they're all versatile enough to feel fresh despite them also containing the basic atk speed or size ? I just really wish more roguelites would have an endless "trial" after your run, to see how far you could actually scale with your current build setup... I know it's pain and ass to balance, it should be really more like a cherry on top, I'm just a very longterm motivated person - balancing of later levels sucks - merging weapons seems impossible for the 5th slot. you want to keep it open for a combination? you'll waste 50k+ gold to reroll 'cuz you only get stuff you don't own yet which also doesn't combine. no, not weapons u can still level, ofc those won't show up - achivements are even worse - so far into the game I'm beginning to regret the invested time

Good enough survivors-like to have on the background, the weapon fusions are fun to discover and use, the farming routine during the runs makes it a little more interesting and motivating to play, the frog roster is relatively versatile, some of it plus the trophies are sometimes tricky to unlock (considering the absence of the endless mode, hence the constant urgency to squeeze in the challenge completion before the 15 minute mark), although once you figure out the formula, max out the stat bonuses and complete every level/difficulty - the challenge is pretty much complete and all that's left is testing out the remaining frogs and completing some more runs for the achievements - which at that point is only a matter of time, rather than strategizing and minmaxing, - which is chill and is much appreciated. Not sure if the upcoming game can make things more spicy, I'll keep an eye on it in any case, and maybe try it out as well, - good to have something relatively engaging to run around in with the option to turn off your brain to and/or play while listening to whatever you like.

This is the first game I've ever gotten %100 on, and I'm so glad the developer is making another one.

This is one of my favorite takes on the bullet heaven genre. It stands out with some original ideas and gameplay, while still being pretty true to the core idea. You have day and night cycles, with some upgrade choices that impact those, and each new day clears the screen (besides bosses) and opens the shop. You plant, water, grow, and harvest crops for XP, kill enemies / mine rocks / fish for coins, and use those coins at the shop to buy crops (including weapon seeds) and pets (which help with tasks) It's pretty active in a way despite not even having a dodge, because you have to move near these things and let the process go while also dodging / killing enemies. It can get HECTIC. But it's fun, and while a lot of the choices are + 1 archtype -1 another, you can mix and match to some extent. Also the different frogs have VERY different build styles which helps keep it interesting

Pesticide Not Required is one of those games that immediately becomes interesting because of how unusual its ideas sound when described together. Farming and bullet heaven gameplay are genres that normally operate in completely different spaces. One focuses on relaxation, slow progression, and resource management, while the other revolves around chaos, overwhelming enemy swarms, and constant action. Surprisingly, instead of fighting against each other, these systems work together in a way that gives the game its own identity. Rather than creating a farming simulator with combat elements or a survivor-style game with light gardening mechanics, the experience feels like a genuine attempt to merge both concepts into a single interconnected gameplay loop. The game places players in an environment where survival extends beyond defeating enemies. While waves of aggressive creatures constantly threaten the player, there is also a growing farm to manage and resources to collect. This creates an experience where progression comes from several directions at once. Defeating enemies remains important, but planting crops, gathering materials, fishing, and expanding available options become equally meaningful. The result is a rhythm that feels busier and more engaging than many traditional survivor-style games because there is almost always another objective competing for attention. One of the strongest qualities of Pesticide Not Required is how productive every activity feels. Farming systems are not treated as decorative additions that simply exist to fit the game's theme. Crops and gathered resources directly support advancement and contribute to future growth. Mining and fishing serve similar purposes, becoming important parts of progression rather than optional distractions. This creates a satisfying cycle where nearly every action pushes players toward some form of improvement. Whether harvesting resources or eliminating enemies, there is a constant feeling that progress is being made. Build customization also appears to play a major role in maintaining long-term appeal. Like many roguelites, the game encourages experimentation through upgrades, traits, and evolving character setups. Runs can develop in very different directions depending on player choices and discovered combinations. Some players may focus entirely on offensive destruction and flood the screen with damage, while others might lean toward gathering efficiency, defensive setups, or more unusual combinations that blend several mechanics together. Discovering powerful synergies and watching strategies evolve over time creates much of the excitement that keeps these types of games enjoyable. Replay value is strengthened further by the game's variety of characters and progression options. Different characters introduce distinct traits and starting conditions that change how players approach each run. Instead of repeating the same routine repeatedly, players are encouraged to adapt and experiment. Different strengths and abilities naturally push players toward playstyles they may not have considered before. This variation helps prevent the experience from becoming repetitive even after multiple sessions. Another enjoyable aspect comes from the inclusion of pets and supportive systems that gradually help automate certain tasks. Early runs may require players to personally handle nearly every responsibility, but progression eventually introduces assistance that makes managing the growing chaos feel more efficient. Watching a small operation slowly evolve into a highly effective system creates a rewarding feeling similar to management games where gradual growth becomes one of the central pleasures. The visual presentation also suits the game's personality well. Pixel-art environments and colorful effects create a style that feels approachable and energetic. Despite large numbers of enemies and effects appearing on screen, the presentation maintains a lighthearted atmosphere that fits the game's unusual blend of farming and action. The simple visual approach also helps maintain readability during intense moments where screens can quickly become filled with movement and chaos. However, the game's many interconnected systems may initially create a learning curve for some players. Managing farming activities, selecting upgrades, gathering resources, and surviving combat encounters simultaneously can feel overwhelming at first. Players looking for a purely straightforward survivor experience might need some time to adjust to the larger number of decisions happening during each run. Certain builds and strategies may also appeal more strongly than others depending on personal preferences. Despite these small concerns, Pesticide Not Required succeeds because it avoids becoming another familiar entry in the increasingly crowded survivor genre. Instead of relying solely on endless enemy waves and upgrade selection, it introduces additional systems that meaningfully affect progression and create a stronger sense of involvement. For players who enjoy roguelite action games and want something that offers more variety beyond simple survival mechanics, Pesticide Not Required delivers a surprisingly addictive experience. It combines relaxation and chaos in a way that initially seems unusual but quickly proves to be one of the game's greatest strengths. Rating: 9/10

I really enjoy this game. To be honest, I’ve never been into survival or roguelike games before, but this one completely won me over. The main character being a frog immediately caught my attention ₍𝄐 ̫𝄐₎ It starts off feeling really calm, almost like a peaceful farming sim where you’re planting crops, fishing, and doing a bit of mining while just living your little frog life. But that relaxing rhythm slowly turns into something more intense when waves of bugs start showing up and you have to defend your farm. What I like is that you don’t use traditional weapons or anything serious, you’re using funny farming tools like lawnmowers and hay bales that end up absolutely shredding everything on screen, which makes the combat feel both silly and satisfying. As you play more, the game opens up a lot. There are different frogs you can unlock, and each one has unique skills and stat changes, so every run feels a bit different. You also get pets that help you with farming tasks like planting, watering, and fertilizing crops, and some even help in combat or collect loot for you. Between runs, you can upgrade your frog’s house, decorate your space, and improve your garden, which gives you something to work toward even after a short session. The farming, fishing, and mining systems also connect into progression. Farming helps you get new weapons and upgrades, fishing is great for early leveling, and mining gives you extra money so you can keep buying seeds and expanding your setup. After each wave, you also get random stat upgrades, so you’re constantly adjusting your build depending on what the game gives you. Even though it’s my first survival style game, it feels really casual and addictive in a good way.

This was the game that started me down the path of bullet heavens — it was a genre I was aware of but didn’t really grab me, but this game pulled me in with the cute art and farm elements, and kept me with incredible gameplay and really unique mechanics. This and Army of Ruin were the first games in the genre I played, and unfortunately I may have played the two best ones first. Alas. I had this same problem with Hollow Knight and metroidvanias. In PNR, you are a smol froggie, and your goal is to protect your farmstead from insect invasion. You do this by farming, mining, and fishing to gain exp, and then growing weapon plants to use as attacks and upgrades. You can also buy or earn farm animals who all help with different farm tasks. The farming mechanics are really, really well-implemented, and make the game very unique in the genre. Choosing whether to focus on farming, mining,or fishing or whether to be a generalist completely shapes your strategy in the run, from which crops you plant to which animals you recruit, and each of the 25ish frogs genuinely requires a different playstyle. The weapons all have their plusses and minuses (I was entertained to find one of the big guides and I really disagreed on what the best weapons were, a great sign for the gameplay), and while certain frogs can aim at certain goals better than others, all of them have their moments, even the more gimmicky ones like James Pond. The game was honestly just a blast. I had runs where I just eked out a win, but the ones where you’d absolutely go off for the last few waves were so satisfying. I’ve been walking around the house lovingly talking about how much fun “the frog game” was for weeks now; I’m excited to see what this dev does next, because they have a real understanding of gameplay design.
